Mr. MAURICE BRASSET (Gaspe) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 36, to amend the Bankruptcy Act (Locality of a debtor).

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Explain.

The object of the amendment is to repeal subsection one of section 4 of the Bankruptcy Act and to substitute therefor the following subsection:
Subject to the conditions hereinafter specified, if a debtor commits an act of bankruptcy a creditor may present, to the court having jurisdiction over the locality of the debtor, a bankruptcy petition.

Unemployment Continuance Act-Closure
The object of the subparagraph added is to remove the handicap under which a debtor is when an assignment is made at a great distance from his place of business and to avoid additional expenditure in the winding up of the estate.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
FRANCE-FOREIGN WHEAT QUOTA On the orders of the day:

About a week ago France undertook to raise to 35 per cent the quota of foreign wheat used in the preparation of bread flour. I noticed in yesterday's newspapers a despatch intimating that on the 27th instant a further arrangement had been made increasing the quota to 40 per cent. May I ask if the government has any information in regard to this matter, and in both cases, the 35 and the 40 per cent, what percentage, if any, of this is Canadian wheat?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The government has been kept informed as to the decrees that have been passed by the French executive and the figures that have been received by the Department of External Affairs from the representatives of Canada in Paris would indicate that purchases of Canadian wheat during the past year had exceeded 31,000,000 bushels, or twice the quantity that had been purchased in any one of recent years. The exact effect of the decree upon immediate importations is, of course, not known and cannot be known until its operations are apparent.

Fortunately, Mr. Speaker, the carrying of the closure motion does not prevent us from drawing to the attention of the country that closure is being applied in this case for one reason and one reason only, and that is to permit the government of Canada to legislate by order in council, so that the government may do in the east block the things which they ought to do in this house of parliament. The government is asking for a blank cheque to spend the money as it pleases, and not in the interests of the unemployed. This is but one more evidence of the fact that the Conservative party and this government is again attempting to play petty politics with the unemployment situation in this country. They want to make it appear to the public that they are really sincere in their professions that they want to do something for the unemployed and that they are being blocked by the opposition, but, Mr. Speaker, the people have been too often deceived by such tactics on the part of the Conservative party to take any stock in such representations again. The people are aware that the leader of the Liberal party, even before this debate began, urged the government to bring down a supply bill to provide an adequate sum for unemployment and farm relief and assured the Prime Minister that if such a measure were brought down it would speedily pass the house. The people are also aware that that offer has since been repeated many times from this side of the house. Indeed, with the acquiescence of the Liberal party in this house I had the honour to make to the government as late as March 11 last, this offer, that if they would bring down a measure to appropriate a sum sufficient to take care of unemployment and farm relief in this country we would pass it within the hour. The government persists in telling the unemployed that they will receive nothing unless the parliament of Canada hands over its powers to the cabinet in council. They persist in telling them that distress will not be relieved unless by a measure coupled with provisions for peace, order and good government. Well, they have had some peace, and a little order, but we have seen no evidence of their good government.
The proposal now before us gives no assurance to the unemployed that one penny of the proposed expenditure will be spent on

their behalf. It simply gives to the government the right to say whether or not they will do anything for tihe relief of the distressed. Why keep the unemployed in suspense?
Hear, hear.
Why, why?
Mr. Speaker, there is one very significant fact about hon. members opposite: They have no constructive suggestions to make, but-
This ought to be good.

-but they are always making ignorant cat calls, heckling and using abusive language. Then when hon. members on this side of the house give them a little of it, Hansard will show that they cringe and whine and ask for the protection of the rules of the house.
Why keep the unemployed in suspense? Why not bring in a measure, now?
That is what we are asking.

Mr. Speaker, last year I had to threaten to keep order myself; I hope I shall not have to follow that course this year. Why not bring down a bill so that this government may do even some little thing, in an endeavour to redeem some of the pledges they made in the year 1930?
What about the five cent piece?

Up to the present time this government has done little except to supplement the efforts of the provinces and the municipalities. Hon. members opposite have encouraged and induced provinces and municipalities to proceed with large expenditures on public works, and at the present time those smaller communities are unable to go farther. Those contracts were undertaken because encouragement had been given by this government, and they were told they would receive assistance. Indeed, on the one hand they did receive assistance to the extent of approximately $50,000,000, while on the other hand the provinces and municipalities were forced to commit themselves to the extent of over $100,000,000.
I repeat that if this measure were to become law to-day we have no assurance that the farmers and the unemployed would receive one cent. Such a measure would simply hand over to the government of Canada powers which they might use at their own discretion, and they would be in a position to decide

whether or not one dollar would be spent. If the government adheres to the principle it has already adopted, namely to supplement only what the provinces and municipalities do, I say, "God take care of the unemployed of this country," because many of the provinces and municipalities are to-day on the verge of bankruptcy. I fear the unemployed will be disappointed just as they were last spring, summer and fall. Why cannot the government bring in a supply bill providing an amount sufficient to attend to the needs of the unemployed? Parliament should be given an opportunity to vote a specific sum so that those in distress may have some assurance that they will receive substantial assistance.
Many excuses have been offered by members of the government as to why the present and no other procedure should be followed. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) gives one excuse, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) gives another, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) yet another. I submit any one of the excuses given by ministers of the crown is ample reason why this government should not be entrusted with the powers they seek. Government supporters, many of my hon. friends opposite, who are now laughing, know very well that this government is taking a wrong step. Knowing that, they have busied themselves in an effort to make people believe the opposition has been blocking the relief measure. My reply to that is that the people have been deceived too often by the tactics of the Conservative party to believe any such suggestion. They were deceived in 1930. In that year the Conservative party promised that if returned to power they would end unemployment. They were deceived when unemployment increased as it still continues to increase. The people were deceived when the Conservative party promised that the unemployment problem would be dealt with on a national basis. The deception was completed when this government would do nothing except supplement the efforts of provinces and municipalities. On the one hand the people thought that this government had assisted the provinces and municipalities to the extent of about $50,000,000. They found however on the other hand that they had been deceived because this government withheld public works, old age pensions, technical education and national highways contributions to the extent of over $60,000,000.
We are asked by this measure to hand to the governor in council the rights of parliament, to trust to the discretion of a government which has already attempted to make

Unemployment Continuance Act
a mockery of parliament. Hon. members are brought from every part of Canada and faced with a measure which deprives them of their rights. We are asked, in a period of distress, when people want work, to give up the powers which parliament possesses. We are asked to trust to a party which treats with scorn, disdain, abuse and heckling any constructive suggestion offered by hon. members on this side of the house. We are asked to trust a party which said in the year 1930, "We want no conferences; we want to give the people work. If we are elected to power we will give them work." Now, when all their policies have failed and they have brought bankruptcy on some provinces and municipalities, they cry out for a conference. We are asked to trust a government that on the floor of this house promised to insist on the payment of fair wages on all public works to which federal funds were contributed. Yet after parliament prorogued this government made agreements with the provinces providing for a maximum instead of a minimum wage and stood idly by while the government of Ontario reduced the rate of wages on such works in northern Ontario to thirty cents an hour, although in the constituency of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) the federal government paid forty cents an hour for the same kind of work. We are also asked to trust a government whose Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) has admitted that he has reduced the wages of men working on our canals. But he did more than that; he established certain classifications and grades by which the wages of those men could be still further reduced, and when this retrograde step was brought to his attention he enunciated a principle that I have never heard before in this house- that the government proposes to pay not one cent more than private employers are paying for similar work. In other words, if private employers take advantage of the times to treat labour as a commodity and drive men into slavery-and many employers are doing this-then the government is prepared to follow suit. We are asked to trust a government the head of which promised that if elected he would make everyone in this country prosperous; but when all his policies failed he went to the city of Toronto and told the people there that it was only by the grace of God that we could be saved; and then he comes to this house after making that declaration and asks for a blank cheque in order to try to save the country himself. Yes, we are asked to trust a government that during the last election organized the unemployed, furnished them with white ribbons
to wear in their lapels, and sent them in to meetings to hiss and jeer at the then Prime Minister and his candidates, and to attend meetings of the Conservative candidates to cheer the great doctor that was to cure all their ills. But after the election when those same men marched to Ottawa to ask for work they were met at the gates of these grounds by an armed force. These same men who in 1930 were told that they were good honest citizens and simply wanted a chance to work, in 1932 are designated as communists and radicals and not to be trusted. How can anyone who has ever given a thought to labour affairs expect that a Conservative government will grapple successfully with any of the problems of the workers? They never have yet, and I do not expect they ever will solve the problems of our workingmen. It is only recently that this government has been converted to the idea of even suggesting any help for the workers. During the 1930 elections the Prime Minister told the people of Guelph: Never trust a convert to do anything that he has not been brought up to do, because he will always make a mess of it.

We have heard that forty
times.
I will give it to you forty-one times.
Order.

The Prime Minister enunciated the principle, "Never trust a convert." I say he is right in that principle, because the Conservative party has only recently been converted to try to do anything for the unemployed.
You are a convert yourself; you were elected first as a Labour member.

What is more, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative party surely has made a mess of the unemployment situation in this country. We are asked to trust a government that never was able to grapple with labour problems without making a mess of them. The other day the Prime Minister told us about the great victory of the Conservative party in the Athabaska by-election.
Hear, hear.

gentlemen to desist from interrupting. Members in this debate are limited to twenty minutes, and even if they are given all their time without interruption they may not be able to say all they want to say.
Hear, hear.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker; it will not take me many more minutes to tell all I want to tell about this government.
I submit that we could not possibly trust this government-a government that went down into Quebec and the maritime provinces and deceived the old people by promising them that if returned to power they would treat old age pensions as a federal obligation. This induced the governments of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to postpone taking pensions and as .a result of the failure of this government to redeem its promise the old people of those provinces lost the benefit of old age pensions. We cannot trust these autocrats to do anything. I say to them:	Bring in a
supply bill even at this late date and give us an opportunity to provide for unemployment and farm relief; bring in a supply bill and we will pass it this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I desire

again to emphasize that in common with every member on this side of the house I am ready and willing and anxious to help the government pass any reasonable supply bill if it is introduced in a constitutional manner; but, so far as I can prevent it, I am not willing to allow any measure to be passed in the autocratic manner in which the government is attempting to force their proposals through the house. If we as members are here for any good purpose it is to try to hand on to those who come after us the free representative institutions which we now enjoy. The freedom which we and every other country enjoy under British parliamentary institutions is due to the sacrifices of our ancestors, and it is our duty to make similar sacrifices for those who succeed us. What difference does it need to make to us personally if conditions in this country are never any better? It will only be a few short years until we too are off the scene. So that if we are here for any good purpose whatever it is to hand on to those who come after us that degree of freedom and liberty which we now enjoy. If we are here for any other purpose, it would be better for ourselves and for our country if we were a thousand miles away.
After ihe convincing manner in which my honoured leader presented the whole question on Tuesday last there was no good reason why the Prime Minister should not have withdrawn his resolution and introduced a supply bill, had he wished to proceed in a constitutional manner. However, he has shown in the most unmistakable way that he is always ready to ride roughshod over the rights of parliament, and he is setting precedents which may guide and direct Canadian parliaments in the days that are to come. The Prime Minister asked this house if it did not agree that in the main the relief measures of the government had worked fairly satisfactorily. An honest review of the facts should tell him that they have been dismal failures.
What are the facts of the matter? Briefly stated, they are these:	The Prime Minister,
appealing to the electorate at Sarnia, Ontario, in July, 1930, said:
Canada is now in a critical condition. Unemployment exists on a scale never before known in the history of this country. AH by reason of the policies of the Mackenzie King government.
At Moncton, New Brunswick, in July of 1930, he said:
Mr. King promises you conferences. I promise you action. He promises you consideration of the problem of unemployment.
I promise to end unemployment. Which plan do you like best?

At Montreal on June 26, 1930, he said: Unemployment has become ia national problem in Canada. The first duty of the Canadian government is to provide work for Canadians.
Mark you, Mr. Speaker; he said this was the first duty of the Canadian government. According to the words of the Prime Minister, unemployment had ceased to be a municipal and provincial problem and had become a national problem, which should be deafit with in a national way. He did not then say "I will hand to some other authority the power to deal with this matter." No; he said, "I promise to end unemployment" and the electorate took him at his word. He called the special session of September, 1930, presumably to end unemployment by federal means, and at that session he jammed through a vote of $20,000,000 presumably for that purpose. But in as little time as it takes to tell he scrapped the whole theory of ending unemployment by federal means, and saddled upon the municipalities and the provinces more than 75.4% of the entire burden. No time was given for discussion; this vote and the changes in the tariff, were forced through parliament by the threat that until these measures were passed the Prime Minister would refuse to leave Ottawa to attend the Imperial conference. Every member of the Liberal party wanted to facilitate, and in fact did facilitate, his going to that conference, but subsequent events have demonstrated that it would have been a good thing for this country if the Prime Minister could have been tied hand and foot so he could not have left. It would have saved this country a lot of humbug.
Time went on, and as the right hon. gentleman continued his policy of humbug, the number of unemployed increased from 117,000 in September of 1930 to 379,000 in October of 1931. Now, according to the estimates of the trades and labour council, the number of unemployed has reached the appalling total of over 550,000, and every sensible person knows that throughout the country there are thousands of people not included in those figures. Then the session of 1931 was called on March 12, and we found that unemployment conditions were infinitely worse than ever before. Every hon. member expected to hear something from the government as to what was being done and what would be done in order to grapple with the situation.
I rise to a point of order.
For four and a half months, from March 12 to July 29-
The hon. member has risen to a point of order.
I have only twenty minutes, Mr. Speaker, and we know my hon. friend sufficiently-
Order.
Just between the pages my hon. friend is turning-
State your point of order.

I am going to state it, and I do not need a prayer book to help me. The hon. member always protests when an hon. gentleman on this side reads his speech, and I protest against my hon. friend reading his speech.
I have not observed the hon. member reading his speech.

I am within your judgment, Mr. Speaker, when I say that scarcely an hon. member rises to speak without keeping his notes either in his hand or on his desk. There is only one reason why I have my notes before me; this is the worst place on earth in which to speak, and sometimes it gets on my nerves.
Then do not protest when others read their speeches.

For four and a half months from March 12 to July 29 we were balked at every turn in our efforts to obtain from the government information which was long overdue. Even in the face of the solemn pledge of the Prime Minister that he would end unemployment by federal means we were continually sidetracked, either by dead silence on the part of members of the cabinet or by such expressions as, "This question can stand," or "The hon. member will be advised when this comes down," or "The matter is purely a provincial one," or "The primary responsibility rests on the provinces and munic>
palities." In this way the chosen representatives of the people were cajoled by the delusive speeches and promises of hon. members opposite. Finally, on July 29, four working days before the session closed, with estimates totalling millions of dollars waiting to be passed and with other important business still before the house, the Prime Minister introduced this blank cheque proposition. No one can be criticized for saying that this measure was brought down in the dying days of the session, when the thermometer was hovering around 110 degrees and when members were so exhausted that they were not in proper condition to give it the serious attention it

Unemployment Continuance Act
demanded. Nevertheless the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), in defending this legislation, stated that it had been given full consideration. At all events, chapter 58 clothed the government with authority to do whatever they liked and expend any amount of money they thought necessary, with no effective check whatever by the Auditor General, the one official who cannot be dismissed by the government without a two-thirds vote of the members of the House of Commons, but who can only exercise his powers when supply is brought down in the regular manner and earmarked for a special purpose. Under this plan -the Auditor General is not allowed to exercise his supervision. On this point the Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
I invite the house to consider that when an appropriation is passed under supply the purpose for which it is used must be specified, and the Auditor General and other officers of the crown, in scrutinizing such expenditures, always keep the government very closely to the purpose specified in such vote.
That was where the shoe pinched; this government, in their reckless extravagance, did not want to be curbed, so through this blank cheque legislation they managed to accomplish their purpose. It was amusing to be told by the Prime Minister that in order to revive this dead statute it was only necessary to use another of his phrases and say, "notwithstanding such and such a condition." Well, sir, if there is anyone who can make black appear white through his phrases, the Right Hon. R. B. is certainly the gent who can do it. He reminds me of the two old Scotchmen who were conversing outside the door of a country crossroads inn. Sandy said to Donal, "I say Donal, d'ye ken what 'Meetaphysics' means?" "No!" said Donal, "I dinna ken." "Well," said Sandy, "just listen and I'll tell you. If you're trjhn' to tell me about something you know nothing about and I know nothing about it either, that's Meetaphysics. And for half your time you are surely guilty of talkin' aboot the likes o'that."
But now, forsooth, as another reason for asking that this act be further extended the Prime Minister wishes a fair application of the test:	"Has this act not worked fairly
well?" The answer is, that the shameful manner in which some of the provinces have misspent these unemployment relief funds granted from the federal chest, should forever damn such an unsound and indefensible system of financing. It is another vindication of the stand which Mr. Mackenzie King and the Liberal party have always taken, namely, that it is a sad mistake to encourage a system 
whereby one authority shall provide the funds for another authority to expend without any responsibility for their provision.
Listen again to the words of the Prime Minister of British Columbia. The British Columbia government launched its program, employed 16,000 men, built 170 camps and contracted a cost of over $50,000 a day on the definite assurance of the federal government that it would pay half the cost. The scandalously lavish manner in which their camps were constructed surpasses all reasonable comprehension. Supplies of all kinds were purchased, including 50,000 blankets and over 100 Delco Light plants; and 450 steel wheel barrows were counted at one camp. A foreman had to be appointed to regulate their use. Men got jobs as surveyors whose fathers held high government positions. Other men, with cars, were running about the country with instruments, to lay out bunkhouses, and erect elevated water supply tanks, where no suitable water supply could be found.
To show further on what a lavish scale the money was handled, they built two camps, only a mile apart. Coal was shipped from Vancouver island for fuel purposes, while lots of suitable wood was lying upon the roadside. Is it any wonder that ultimately orders were received from the federal authorities that such extravagance must cease? But not until over $3,500,000 had been expended in this scandalously extravagant manner. Machinery was bought on a scale never before known in connection with relief work. Take the whole country over. During the sixteen months ending with January 31, 1932, out of the entire expenditure of $146,899,219 only 331,145 workmen were given employment for only some 44i days over the entire sixteen months, or an average of less than 3 days per month. Out of $147,000,000 expended in all, only $35,147,320.80 went for unemployment relief, less than one-third of the entire sum, constituting one of the most scandalously indefensible expenditures ever put over in the whole history of this country. And yet the Prime Minister had the temerity to stand up the other day and tell the house that the scheme had worked remarkably well.
I would like the Prime Minister to tell us where the other $112,000,000 has gone. Verily, were I in his predicament with such a record to my credit I would feel that I ought to be lashed for the remainder of my life.
Take also the administration of that $5,250,000 which has gone to direct relief for those 50,000 families in Saskatchewan, who have been in the burnt-out area for three successive seasons. To think that these people

Unemployment Continuance Act
through no fault of their own should suffer the loss of their all, for three successive seasons, and then at the hands of this government be compelled to sign promissory notes, which may hang over their heads for years. Do the members of this government not know of the carloads upon carloads of fruit, vegetables and provisions sent out this last fall from Ontario for the help of those people- almost eighty per cent of which came from my county of Huron?
No. Mr. Speaker-
Order.

And we were
proud to come to their succour with this gift, for which we charged not a cent. When it comes to providing out of the federal chest by the government of Canada, or in other words through the whole of the people of Canada, they compel these farmers to sign promissory notes. Just picture the situation. Here are 50,000 farmers who have lost their all; yet, sir, they are compelled to sign promissory notes. An election comes on. Suppose I am in the field as a candidate. All I need to do is to send my emissaries all over that section of the country and warn these people of the obligation which hangs over their heads, telling them that they had better realize on which side their bread may be buttered. This is one of the most detestable stipulations which it is possible to think of. These promissory notes ought to be cancelled at once. It is one of the most detestable tricks which any administration could be guilty of, and so far as my voice would carry, 1 would stand here to Domesday to insist that the government withdraw that stipulation. I appeal to the better judgment of every hon. member of this house. I know there are many hon. members sitting across the floor, men who are honestly inclined, who in the ordinary affairs of life would not think of stooping to anything of a questionable nature. Why can we not for once in our lives stand shoulder to shoulder and insist that this government shall at once relieve these people of any such promissory notes?
The hon. member has spoken twenty minutes.
Thank you. Interruptions constitute the argument, Mr. Speaker, which we always get from Tories who have not a case.

Industry is upset; commerce is not only stagnant, but topsy-turvey; capital, accumulated in the hands of the few, is kept hidden behind steel doors; our unemployed are starving and in a state of indescribable misery, while those engaged in the cultivation of the soil-our farmers, the most important class in the community-are unable to sell their products, and in fear of becoming destitute in the midst of plenty. At the same time they are astounded to find that although their barns are filled to capacity many of their fellow Canadians lack the necessaries of life.

He is resourceful in debate, but he made a woeful mess of his case the other day. In the bottom of his heart he knew that he was defending some-tliing in which he did not believe, and his defence of the government was rather pitiful to hear. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) also defended the government in one of his fiery stump speeches which perhaps would have sounded better out on the hustings than in this House of Commons. But what about the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie)? Should he not be here to defend this legislation? The Minister of Justice is perhaps the minister who should bear the brunt of a debate such as this. I would not expect the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) to defend this legislation, though the other day the Prime Minister said, almost with tears in his eyes, that opposition members were criticizing the cabinet because they did not assert themselves. The Prime Minister said, "I want to tell the house and the country that we have many differences at cabinet meetings; we do not always see eye to eye. I have great difficulty with some members of the cabinet."
I should like to know who are those members. Can anyone imagine the Minister of Public Works combating the Prime Minister? Can anyone imagine even the Minister of Justice, in this late day, when he is nearing the end of his political career and is looking forward to something else, combating the Prime Minister? It is quite obvious that the Minister of Labour never combated the Prime Minister or he would not have been elevated to his present office. They take it lying down and sitting up; there is one man at the head of this government all the time, and that is the right hon. Prime Minister. Then I come to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sutherland) who is a good friend of mine. I do not think he ever combated the Prime Minister. The great trouble, Mr. Speaker, is that the government are in a 41761-93J
hole; they know that is so, and they are in that hole because of their own blunders. The record of this government has been one blunder after another since they took office on August 7, 1930, and they are now asking for sympathy. They say that the opposition is criticizing them and they are pleading for sympathy. They do not deserve any sympathy and I can assure them that they are not going to get any sympathy from the people of this dominion anywhere from coast to coast. The people are going to seize the first opportunity they have to turn them out of office because they came in on promises which they have broken and they have carried on the most bungling government we have ever had in this country.

Let me say to hon. gentlemen who are jeering over there that they have not the courage to get up and defend this legislation. I could name some of those gentlemen but I will not honour them by doing so. They are the most docile lot of sheep I ever saw. They will follow this government everywhere, although they would like to vote against the government. Many of them at the bottom of their hearts would like to vote against the government to-night, but they are afraid that if they did so the government would be defeated and they would not get back here again. The result is that they are following their leader everywhere. They are following the miracle man, the superman, the man who has been overcoming difficulties all his life and who thrives on difficulties; and here we have him attempting to enact in this parliament a piece of legislation the like of which has never been heard of.
There is more I could say about the Prime Minister. My hon. friend from South Essex (Mr. Gott) said that I had criticized the hon. gentleman in London, Ontario. Perhaps I did criticize the Prime Minister, and I will criticize him whenever I have reason to do so. Who is he that he should not be criticized? My hon. friends are afraid of him; every member of the cabinet is afraid of him. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) is a very large man but his courage fails him when he comes up against the Prime IVJinister; his courage oozes right out, And that holds true of all members of the cabinet. This debate

That hon. gentleman has been put up to defend the government, but not a cabinet minister gets up to perform that duty. What is this government coming to? What is the country coming to? Is the Minister of Labour tongue-tied? Is the Minister of Trade and Commerce tongue-tied? I see the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Murphy) is in; is he tongue-tied? Are they all tongue-tied? The superman, the boss, has said, "No one shall speak to-night," and they are not speaking-that is, except the hon. gentleman from South Essex who got up to make a wonderful speech. My hon. friend from Toronto East Centre (Mr. Matthews) speaks out; he says they are watching me. Well, we are watching him until he steps up as lieutenant-governor of Ontario. He will be very docile at all times. Is there any other hon. gentleman who would like to say anything over there? If I had unlimited time I would take on the whole crowd to-night, but I have not the time.
Let me say, in closing, what has been said many times from this side in regard to this matter. This supergovernment could bring in a supply bill to-night for $50,000,000 or 8100,000,000 or any amount they might want and we would pass it in half an hour. What are they afraid of? The Prime Minister likes to speak of peace, order and good government; he likes to refer to the mother of parliaments and the British constitution and to talk about peace, order and good government. We have peace in this country, Mr. Speaker, and we have order in this country; but I cannot say that we have good government in this country. No ong can say that; no one will say it unless it be the members of the government themselves.

I was saying that I hold in my hand a copy of The New Despotism, and as I look across the floor of the house and see men who are supposed to be the representatives of the Canadian people, but who stand for a policy of constitutional despotism and are followers of a despotic Prime Minister,

Unemployment Continuance Act
and when I look at the resolution before the house and note the phraseology in which that despotic resolution is clothed, I wonder just what hon. gentlemen opposite think of themselves. They are trying to tell the people of Canada that there is an exceptional emergency in this country. They are trying to tell the people of Canada that we must have this type of legislation because a national disaster is facing them. That is all nonsense; no national disaster is facing Canada except the disaster of bad government brought into existence by hon. gentlemen opposite during the last two years.
One begins to wonder just why we have more than a hundred members of parliament from all parts of Canada sitting still and saying practically nothing when such an important question in regard to unemployment and farm relief is before us. Although for the last three weeks in the house we have had a debate on this problem, only infrequently has a minister or a private member opposite had the courage to tell the riding he represents and the people of Canada just where he stands on this proposition. If we read the resolution, we find in the first line the significant word "expedient." It states: Resolved that it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend a certain chapter and to strike out a certain word and substitute another word therefor. When we come to consider just what the government is trying to do, the word "expedient" has certainly an important significance. What is it? One explanation of the word is that it is "a shift made to make the best of things," and I believe the government is to-night trying to put forward a type of legislation that will enable it to get out of a bad hole. But when this fight is carried to the electors, as it will be two or three years from now, I am badly mistaken if the government will not be sorry for ever attempting, as they have done, to rush through the house such a piece of arrogant legislation.
Again, the term "expedient" is "a device or contrivance to serve in lieu of something better." It is "something characterized by mere utility rather than principle," and, indeed, there is not much principle to the government's move. Further, it is "an objective conducive to special advantage rather than what is universally admitted to be right." That makes me wonder why the Prime Minister, his cabinet and all the members sitting behind them will attempt to defend a policy that seeks to attain an objective that is not in the best interests of this country at the present time in the way of unemployment and farm relief.
As a member from western Canada I am ready to vote now, before this question is put, any sum of money that is necessary for relief and unemployment in Canada. I am, however, very anxious to make it plain that as a member from a riding in western Canada I shall not stand for a type of government that will want me, as a representative of a free riding, to delegate legislative authority from this chamber to a cabinet that will by order in council override the commons and practically annihilate what is left of responsible government in this country. I am not ready to do that, and for that reason I am opposing this legislation. I am ready to take a stand on it and to carry this fight into my riding for the next two or three years. If other hon. members will do the same, then, when the government goes to the country, no matter what other questions there may be, this will not be a forgotten issue. I think it is now generally conceded among Conservatives themselves that if the house were dissolved to-night and the people were left to pronounce the verdict, the government opposite would be defeated by at least fifty of a majority.

Why talk about peace when there is no peace? Why talk about order when I believe one of the real reasons for the introduction of this resolution is that the Prime Minister is afraid of a national uprising in Canada? He is afraid the labour people and the communists are going to give trouble. Consequently, he wants to have at hand the power of a despot to crush any movement that may arise. The very fact that the Prime Minister believes this proves that he is not in touch with public opinion. There is no fear of any such thing in this country; there is no possible danger in that direction. Therefore one is lost in trying to find out just what the ideas of hon. gentlemen are in introducing vicious legislation of this kind.
This sort of legislation is foreign to any parliament in any British dominion. It is foreign to any legislation enacted by the home government. We are told that free institutions are the lifeblood of the empire. Yet we have hon. gentlemen opposite, who on the hustings are always saying how they stand for the dear old empire and for the old Union Jack, giving us the spectacle of supporting in the House of Commons legislation that is not in any sense of the word symbolical of free institutions. Free institutions are the lifeblood of the empire; free cooperation is the instrument of the empire and peace, order and progress, the objectives of the empire. Yet how are we going to attain those objectives of the empire when we resort to legislative tactics of this kind in our national parliament?
If I read my history aright, the whole battle in Canada for hundreds of years was to win responsible government. We had throughout the French .period governor after governor, intendant after intendant, bishop after bishop, council after council, doing what? Representing French imperialism, and through their action and interaction with one another throughout ' that period, very little was accomplished. But they did this much: they laid the foundation in that probationary period, of responsible government in the dominion, and we are building on that historic foundation to-day. Later, in Upper Canada the fight was against a legislative council that was not responsible to the .people; in Lower Canada the fight was the same. In New Brunswick, in Nova Scotia and in Prince Edward Island the same battle had to be fought to win for us the boon of responsible government. Yet to-night, Mr. Speaker, we have a motion before the house by which the government is practically trying to drive its thoughtless legislation through by what we might call gag rule. When we think of the splendid con-
(Mr. McIntosh.]
tributions that have been made by the different parts of this dominion in days gone by in the cause of responsible rule, I am sure that we ought all to be concerned, irrespective of party, for the future of constitutional government in this country.
One of the speakers this afternoon intimated that so far as this particular legislation is concerned there might not be very much danger in it, that we could judge the future by the past. But that is just what we cannot do. We may judge it in a particular way, but I say, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot estimate the future by the past, and I would like to put on record a statement made by one of the assemblies, years ago, in the eastern provinces in respect to that very question. It said:
The assembly admitted that no evil has thus far resulted from the opposition of the council-
That is the legislative council:
-but pointed out that the future could not be anticipated and that there was no deficiency of independent men who had every qualification for seats in the legislative council.
That means, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot constitutionally anticipate the future, and it is utterly impossible for any man who wants to stand by the constitution in this country conscientiously to vote for a piece of legislation of this kind, because if one wants to play fair with the people he cannot give to any government or any cabinet or any prime minister, no matter what its particular political stripe may be, the powers that are being sought under this iniquitous piece of legislation.
I might go from one province to another throughout this whole country to prove conclusively that in the working out of responsible government in this country the policy that is being backed by hon. gentlemen opposite is a futile one and will prove to be a failure. What does Lord Hewart say on this question in his book, The New Despotism, which I hold in my hand? He says that the time has arrived in all the overseas dominions when a tendency has become manifest to hand over to the executive the powers of parliament, and he says that there are three or four excuses given for doing so. One is that it is said that parliament simply has not time to do otherwise than delegate its legislative power; another is that parliament has not the requisite aptitude for the work; another is that the task of government ought to be left to the executive. These three excuses do not amount to anything. They do not constitute a sound reason why we should depart from the principle of responsible government in this dominion. Lord Hewart says as to the third of these propositions, the delegating of legislative power to the cabinet:

Unemployment Continuance Act
As for the third of the propositions, if it contemplates anything over and above what in a particular emergency may be rendered necessary by "sudden causes and occasions" or "promptitude to meet the exigency of the case," it is not easy to imagine anything more mischievous or more subversive.
There is the point exactly, that the minute we hand over the legislative power of parliament to any cabinet or any executive, at that moment we endanger the constitution of this country, and therefore to-night, Mr. Speaker, I am utterly and absolutely opposed to this legislation. I am opposed to the motion before the house. I am opposed to the resolution because I believe that the government, although satisfied that it is in the wrong, is trying to drive this thing through by the sheer force of its majority, and that if it had the courage of its convictions it would even at this late moment back up on its tracks and bring down a regular supply bill which parliament could put through in half an hour or so, thereby bringing to bear upon the problem of unemployment and farm relief in this country the necessary responsible parliamentary authority.
In closing, may I say that so far as western Canada is concerned I do not believe that the action of the government will be in any way popular. I believe that the rank and file of the people are opposed to the policy of the government as enunciated in this resolution, and therefore I am only too pleased to have had an opportunity to say what I have said in the house to-night in opposition to it.

prime minister, by the resolution which he has submitted to this house, wishes to revive that pernicious legislation, 'that was devised for the first time in Canada by the conservative party in order to prevent the greatest Canadian that ever sat in this house from upholding the rights of the minority-I refer to the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Mr. Speaker, the right hon. prime minister told us last week that he had been placed
at the head of 'the government by the people and that he still had their support. There are both some truth and untruth in that statement. It is true that he was placed at the head of the government by the people, but how did it happen? If the people gave a confidence vote to the conservative party in the last election, it was on account of the promises made by that party, through its present prime minister; those promises having been repeated by its candidates and the various speakers who supported them. They promised to put an end to unemployment, to secure work for everyone, to open new markets where manufactured and farm products could be sold at a higher price. Thus the manufacturers would have paid higher wages, and at the same time the farmers would have enjoyed greater prosperity, but that has not yet materialized. In our rural districts, the speakers who supported the conservative party, went a little further; they said:	"You
are aware that Hon. R. B. Bennett is an acknowledged business man and an experienced financier; besides, his past proves it." Mr. Bennett is enough of a business man to find money to reorganize your companies, so that all of you, workingmen, may work six days a w^ek with better wages." What happened? Wages went down 40 or 50 per cent since.
It is on account of those promises that the people of this Dominion placed him at the head of the government, but these pledges were never fulfilled. How disappointed he must be to day, when he realizes that they have not materialized, that the condition of agriculture is worse, that unemployment is steadily increasing, in spite of the explicit promises made to the people of this country in 1930. If, in the past, the prime minister showed himself to be a business man-when he was working for himself-it must be a great disappointment for his friends to see that he fell short of his reputation so quickly after his appointment as prime minister. But, to-day, it is a fact, and yet, these hon. members dare to support those who are guilty of such an act and deny what they then said.

May I, sir, at the outset of
my remarks on -this resolution quote, as an introduction, a few sentences of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), taken from his speeches delivered on March 8 and 23 last, when he was discussing this proposed measure, and speaking on the motion of the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir). His comments will give us an insight into the state of mind under which the Prime Minister laboured when he endeavoured to impose on this parliament an act which is contrary to all parliamentary traditions of this country.
On March 8, he stated, when introducing this resolution:
It confers a wide discretion upon the executive; I said so last year, and I repeat it now.
I am not one of those who do not understand and appreciate the attitude of mind taken by the opposition with respect to this question, but I do say with some degree of pride and satisfaction that although that statute came into force in August and we have administered it ever since, you wilt have great difficulty and indeed I think you will find it impossible, sir, to point to any case in which there has been an abuse of authority under it or -where there has not been an honest administration of its provisions.

In his speech on the same motion, he repeats his argument giving it a different form, as follows:
I would not ask this power from any parliament except reluctantly, and I so stated when I introduced the resolution the other day. But, sir, after discussions between my colleagues and myself, and taking into consideration the views expressed to us by others who look at the matter dispassionately and from the outside, dare we as a government, charged with the tremendous responsibility in this emergency of caring for this dominion to the best of our ability, be without that power? We have said, no. We do not believe that this power will be called into play; nay, more, we sincerely and fervently hope that it will not be. But, sir, what is a man without a weapon in the midst of armed force? What is a man who has no instrument for his protection in the midst of the strife of brigands?
The above quotations from the speeches of the Prime Minister indicates clearly that he is conversant with the constitution of our country, that he is familiar with the fundamental principles which must govern our parliamentary life and it is with repugnance, and reluctantly, that he submits to us this resolution.
I listened closely to the speeches delivered by the members of the government and to those who supported them, and it struck me that hon. members opposite seemed to not understand the attitude taken by Liberals on that question. I did not hear one single Conservative member state that it was reluctantly that he supported this violation of our constitution. The right hon. Prime Minister's supporters seemed to pay little attention to his speech, while he, himself, was fully aware to what extreme means he had recourse to impose his will. If we turn over the pages of our history, we shall note that, for over one hundred years, our forbears had to struggle to obtain what is known as self-government. Following the conquest; the military government of 1763, recognized no rights to the Canadian people nor granted any representation in the nation's council. The Quebec act of 1774 acknowledged some privileges to the people of Quebec, or to those who had remained in Canada after the conquest; such as their language, customs and religion. In 1791, the Constitutional Act separated the two provinces and allowed us to have a number of represenatives in the council of the nation, but no control over supply or the taxes levied on our people. In 1837, the rebellion took place, blood flowed in an endeavour to obtain the control of the treasury. Even in 1840, under the Union Act, this responsibility of governments was not

Unemployment Continuance Act
yet achieved; it was only in 1867, by the British North America Act, looked upon by us, from our childhood and youth, as the ideal condition for a people, that we obtained to be represented, to decide how the taxes were to be levied, how we were to limit them and how the disposal of the revenues would be made in the interest of the whole nation. If we study the constitutional history of our country, we will note that in the conventions negotiated between Lower and Upper Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, there seems to be an understanding by which consent of the parties is necessary to enact radical changes in our constitution.
Since 1867, we find but three instances, in the history of our confederation, where the government undertook the responsibility of requesting a fixed amount but without being able however to determine how the funds would be expended. In 1885, during the Riel rebellion, in the west, parliament granted to the government of that day a sum of $1,500,000, so as to crush this rebellion; the amount had been mentioned but without giving details or the information usually required when such amounts are asked.
The second instance in our parliamentary history, when parliament trusted the government by granting them a stipulated amount, but without giving details, goes back to Queen Victoria's Jubilee. The last instance, was in 1914, when the war, in which we took part, was declared. Under the Conservative regime of 1914, parliament granted the government on various occasions during the years of war, large amounts to meet the expenditure of our active participation in the conflict. However, on no occasion did a government think of requesting the house to despoil itself of the rights conferred upon it by the British North America Act. Pursuant to these rights conferred upon us by the Confederation Act, the people's representatives alone, by an unwritten law, have full power over the disposal of the public funds and their duty is to supervise the expenditure of these funds.
Now, we have a Conservative Prime Minister, whose mentality, character and autocratic methods are known, he assumes himself full responsibility and decides that the Conservative party is willing to undertake such a task which may lead to abuses-which the Prime Minister himself admits-and endeavours to deny the supremacy conferred on parliament by the will of the people, in order that he can transfer it to the executive, which is but a committee of -this house.
If you peruse the British North America Act, you will find the powers of the executive defined in sections 9 and 16. If you examine section 17, you will note that the legislative powers reside in parliament which comprises the House of Commons, the Senate and an executive to whom is confided the administration of the laws adopted by the two chambers just mentioned. These powers were never ceded to the government, an extraordinary crisis must exist to force this government to resort to these unheard of methods, even during the period of war, such extreme measures, as to reverse the roles in parliament, were never thought of.
Parliament has the right to legislate on the various matters enumerated in section 91 of the British North America Act. This section confers on parliament the exclusive authority to legislate so as to maintain order, peace and good government in this country. Further on the act enumerates the various matters over which we have the power to legislate. This resolution requests us to admit that the Canadian parliament is incapable of legislating in order to relieve the present crisis; but, in this parliament, there exists a group of men who have all the necessary qualifications, energy and will to govern the country, as a small committee, without making any report to parliament. These are the men who are supposed to relieve the situation.
The first remedy to which they resorted, at the special session of 1930 consisted in the definite amount of $20,000,000. This sum sufficed to meet the emergency during 1930. By voting this S20,000,000, parliament or the house was not asked to renounce its powers. It was in 1931 that a blank signature was requested. It was on July 31, if my memory serves me right, that this bill was discussed in the house, and parliament prorogued on August 3. In the dying days of the session the enactment of this measure was requested, notwithstanding the statement of the leader of the opposition that, if circumstances warranted it, he was ready to sit until the government introduced a bill which would be acceptable to all, because it was quite clear that the bill1 introduced was in violation of the principle of self-government, by virtue of which the house has control over the expenditure made by the government.
By this measure which they wish to thrust upon us, it is contended that means will be found to meet the situation, end unemployment and relieve the people. With this aim in view they state, we have devised the following scheme: we have a group of fifteen or sixteen men who, we think, are much better

endowed than you are and we therefore request that they should be given your authority to legislate.
I often wonder what the electorate think of the government's followers when they witness their attitude on this question. At the next election, I know that, in Quebec, this question will not be a dead issue and the people of that province will prove to the entire country that, at least, they still are attached to the constitution and they will certainly support the representatives who champion their rights. The ridicule which the government attempts to saddle on the opposition, because they champion thoro liberties which were conquered at the price of our blood, the people of Quebec, the whole Dominion will remember. The Canadian people themselves, will discover that the measure, which the Prime Minister wishes to impose on us, leads to many abuses.
One argument put forth in favour of this act is as follows:-We cannot state the amount because we are not aware of the disbursements we will have to make. It is not what the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull) stated some time ago in the city he represents :
The present government will within a few months, have to borrow six or seven hundred million dollars.
He is then aware of the amount necessary to meet the expenditure of his government. How does it happen that an ordinary member can state that next year Saskatchewan will need 826,000,000, that the rebate of five cents per bushel of wheat will amount to $10,000,000 and that the loan to that province will amount to 86,000,000?
If this hon. member is so well acquainted with the requirements of the provinces so as to relieve the present crisis, why should not the government specify an amount, as the leader of the opposition and his followers stated. They could request 8600,000,000, and I think the opposition would agree to that amount, believing sincerely that the government would limit useless expenditure. We could then have some control over the funds disposed of. If 850,000,000 had been voted in 1931, it would have met the situation then existing, since the reports laid on the table of the house show that only $34,000,000 or $36,000,000 were expended. They might, to-dajq if the requirements are greater to relieve the situation, state a definite amount, thus the authority of this parliament and the prerogatives of the house would remain intact. The industrial conditions in our country instead of improving after all the means taken,

is worse than in 1930, and we are also aware that there are more unemployed in Canada, per capita, than in any other country.
I would have been recreant to my duty had I not protested against this legislation which will certainly have disastrous results, since the Prime Minister himself admits that it may pave the way to abuses.

Mr. Speaker I propose to make only a few brief remarks with respect to the measure now before the house. I have always understood that precedents play a most important part in the parliaments within the British empire. Such great importance is attached to precedents that the establishment of any new and important precedent which may have grave and far-reaching effects is a very serious responsibility for any government to undertake. The measure now before the house does constitute a grave and far-reaching precedent. It permits the cabinet to change or amend existing laws and takes away from the House of Commons control over public moneys; indeed it vests almost unlimited authority in the cabinet. This, of course, creates a constitutional issue, and from my observation it is being so considered by the man of the street.
This grave departure from the established order of things has resolved itself into a question as to whether this parliament shall support the old-established order of parliamentary procedure or depart from it as a matter of so-called expediency. The government of the day has made its choice and by invoking closure has plainly indicated that it proposes to stick by that choice. The Liberal party opposes this step by all the means in its power, and I am convinced that when the people become fully aware of all the implications of the step the government is now taking, and of the hollowness of the excuses it offers for so doing, they will make their opinion felt in no uncertain manner.
The other day the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) spoke of the vote of confidence that he and his party had received in the recent by-election in Athabaska. That so-called vote of confidence amounts to less than one third of the total vote cast in the election. If the hon. gentlemen who sit to your right, Mr. Speaker, are content to call that a vote of confidence, we on this side of the house are content that they should do so.
More than once I have heard this debate referred to as a waste of time. That is not correct. This debate has done a great service, if only to establish that the measures the gov-

Unemployment Continuance Act
eminent has taken in conjunction with the provincial governments and the municipalities have not been adequate or successful, even to a small degree, in coping with the depression. Nearly $150,000,000 has been spent and thereby employment amounting to less than one month in a year to each person has been afforded. One member sitting on the government benches said that this expenditure had enabled many people "to keep body and soul together." In my opinion the one thing more than all [DOT]others that has enabled hundreds of thousands of our unemployed to weather the storm as well as they have is the wonderful kindness that Canadian families, still in receipt of an income, have shown to relieve relatives and friends in distress. This should cause a feeling of pride in every Canadian heart. Organized charity is also playing its part nobly, and the time and money that have been given to this great cause will not be soon forgotten by those who have benefited.
I am one of those who believe the government has been actuated by good motives, but the results of the tremendous expenditures of public moneys have been most disappointing, and I think the people are convinced that the policy of the government with regard to unemployment has failed in its object.
I once hoped that state unemployment insurance never would be necessary in Canada, but the efforts of the government in the past two years, during which I have seen so many good citizens suffer the miseries and hardships of unemployment, have about convinced me that the time has come for the government of Canada to explore seriously and sincerely the advisability of bringing down a measure to provide contributory state unemployment insurance suitable to the needs of Canada's army of unemployed men and women, and to the conditions that obtain in Canada, not only now, but during years of prosperity as well. That is a personal opinion, but it is one which I feel must be expressed. It is obvious that such a measure, if it were introduced, would have to be very carefully framed in order to guard against the abuses that are stated to be apparent in the unemployment act of Great Britain. The Dominion government, the provincial governments, and all employers and employees throughout Canada would have to bear their just and equitable share of the cost of such unemployment insurance, but I think all classes in Canada are ready to do so in order that certain and orderly relief may come to those who suffer the tragedy of unemployment.
As I said before, I had hoped that such an enactment might not become necessary in
Canada. It would be costly and it has certain obvious drawbacks, but it would be infinitely better than present conditions. The people of Canada want the money voted for unemployment relief to go into the pockets of those who, through no fault of their own, are unemployed, and not to contractors and so on; and through the unemployed they want this money to go to the small merchants, who need it most in these days. The present policy of the government has shown very clearly that the creation of special jobs is very unsatisfactory and very expensive; this method has been given an extensive trial and has failed to meet the situation. Obviously the government must try another policy if it is to satisfy the people of this country. The Prime Minister has said that Canada will never have the dole, but I take that to mean that the dole will be given as a last resort. We are rapidly approaching that situation, and we cannot afford to further disregard the failure of another "noble experiment."

Mr. Speaker, with respect to the proposed legislation now before the house, which when amended is intended to revive chapter 58 of the statutes of 1931, I have but little to say except to remark that the substitution of a fixed sum for the words "such moneys as the governor in council in his discretion may deem to be necessary," in section 2, and the elimination of the words "and maintain within the competence of parliament, peace, order and good government throughout Canada," in sections 3 and 4, would have made this measure entirely acceptable to the opposition.
I want to speak at greater length with regard to the closure which is to be applied at this time. I was startled when the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) moved closure; I wondered just why that should be done. I thought I might find in the speech of the Prime Minister some substantial reason for this action having been taken, but diligent study of his speech has not rewarded me. I should like to direct attention to a few of the statements made by the right hon. gentleman, and a few of the quotations given by him, which statements and quotations no doubt were intended to give his reasons for applying closure at this time.
The Prime Minister quoted Redlich, and a little later I intend to refer to some of the details of that quotation. In general, however, we were reminded that in the latter part of the nineteenth century there was real, substantial obstruction in the British parliament.

The dangerous nature of that obstruction was pointed out, threatening as it did British parliamentary institutions and established practices. Finally, attention was directed to the steps that were taken to control the situation. Then the Prime Minister inferred that a parallel situation existed in Canada at the present time, and apparently he attempted to justify the guillotine thereby. With the permission of the house I should like to direct attention to the first quotation given by the right hon. gentleman, which is found at page 1404 of Hansard for March 23. This is part of a speech made by the Prime Minister of England, and reported in the proceedings of the special committee on Procedure on Public Business:
Really, what is the House of Commons itself? It consists not only of a government, but of an opposition, and they have both got functions and rights. The great right of the opposition is the full discussion of measures proposed by the government. It is there, I think, that our fundamental weakness lies. There is a doctrine that it is the function of the opposition to oppose. I have always regarded that as a crime against the state.
I should like to direct particular attention to these words:
. . . they have both got functions and rights. The great right of the opposition is the full discussion of measures proposed by the government.
That is exactly the stand taken by the opposition here; we claim that we should have the right to discuss the amount to be expended under the proposed legislation, and that we should be able to discuss and criticize the manner in which it is to be expended, whether in public works at the federal expense, in grants in aid to the provinces to assist them in the carrying on of public works, or in direct relief. Then we should like to discuss whether or not the government should have other powers than merely those of providing relief to the needy, seed grain and feed to the farmers and employment on public works, whether alone or in conjunction with the provinces. We claim that it is not full discussion if we are not to have any voice in the fixing of the amount to be appropriated or in the manner in which that appropriation is to be expended.
The Prime Minister referred to the mother of parliaments, and quoted chapter 48 of the statutes of 1930-31, passed by the British parliament. He pointed out that very large powers were conferred by that statute upon the privy council of England, but close examination of this chapter shows that the only power conferred is the power to make orders affecting certain economies. The closer we

study that chapter the more that view will be confirmed. We should note also that these powers were conferred upon a council that formed the executive of a national and not a party government; that the powers were conferred for one month only, and that the subjects to which they might be applied were only five in number, education, national health insurance, police, unemployment insurance and roads.
The Prime Minister directed attention to one particular clause which gave power to increase or vary the contributions made to the unemployment fund. I am referring now to page 1410 of Hansard. The words of the act are, "For increasing the contributions to be made to the unemployment fund." So, search as you may, you will not find the slightest power to spend money; it only has to do with effecting economies. Within the four corners of that statute will be found no blank cheque and no blanket authority. I wish to refer now to a certain quotation of the Prime Minister's from Red-lich's Procedure of the House of Commons. I shall read only a brief extract from it:
Irreconcilable parties, which oppose an existing union of states or stand for a subordination of state to church, parties which reject the whole framework of society, or which draw their life from a principle only less deep and powerful than that of religion, the principle of nationality, are all in mortal conflict-latent if not apparent, possibly unconscious for long periods-with the conventions of parliament; they are, therefore, knowingly or unknowingly attacking parliamentary government itself, at all events in the form known to the constitution. Obstruction is. in reality, nothing less than a repudiation of the existing constitution of the country, intensified to the point of denying the right of its parliament to exist, and expressed in a conscious misuse of the forms and principles of procedure essential to the efficiency of parliamentary action.
Before making this quotation the Prime Minister used these words:
Reading from the third volume of that work, page 196, I shall now give a description of what has transpired in this house during the last ten days.
In other words, the Prime Minister attributes to the opposition those very things that I have read in your hearing. The paragraph preceding the one from which the Prime Minister quoted begins with these words:
Such is the political atmosphere in which the latest procedure reforms have been produced.
I think it is wise that we should find out what that particular atmosphere was. Many of us who have read the history of the British parliament during that trying period from 1867 to 1902 know that the political

atmosphere was most disturbed all the time. To begin with, there was the burning question of home rule for Ireland; there was the South African policy of the imperialists; there was the imperialist tariff policy, and there was the education question. Probably during the last century no other question had1 disturbed the minds of the British people to the extent that these particular questions did. Take for instance the question of home rule for Ireland. I need not remind hon. gentlemen that for about thirty years this was one of the most vital questions discussed in the British House of Commons. Two years after his election Mr. Parnell became the storm centre of that house. He tried first of all by so-called constitutional means to induce the house to listen to him, but when he found that he was getting nowhere, what did he do? He and his party set out to upset the proceedings of the house. Parnell was called the originator of systematic obstruction, and he certainly was. On one occasion he said, "I feel a special satisfaction in preventing and thwarting the intentions of the government." What happened during those hectic times? On July 31, 1877, O'Donnell, with four others, moved thirteen motions for adjournment. On that occasion the sitting lasted twenty houra and fifteen minutes, and the highest number of the minority at any time during those motions for adjournment was seven. On another occasion the sitting lasted twenty-two hours, the result being 251 votes for the government and 33 for the opposition. But there came a time when the sitting lasted forty-one and one-half hours. On one occasion 132 amendments were moved.
Mr. Speaker, what has this to do with the question before the house?
The difference is that one knows his business and the other's seem to be all mixed up.

As I say, on one occasion in the British house 132 amendments were moved to one clause, and now this closure rule has been invoked here in this parliament to prevent one amendment being moved. The Prime Minister quoted Redlich and I wish to quote from that authority too. Redlich says:
Moreover, the feeling of the universal benefit conferred, as a rule, by strenuous and powerful opposition is one which centuries of experience have worked into the very flesh and blood of the English nation. Over and over again it has been seen that the energetic resistance of a
minority has roused the entire country to take part in political life, and has brought a whole subject up for discussion in all its aspects: hasty measures have been checked, and proposals for large alterations in the law have been made by way of compromise, and in the end have only been partially carried out. The feeling of the need for opposition and the experiences which support it have led to the characteristic tendency of English procedure which finds expression in the strong emphasis placed on the protection of the minority.
I have a much longer quotation but I will not read more. What has been the view of the Prime Minister heretofore, even in the year 1931? At page 4279 of Hansard of July 29.last, the Prime Minister said:
I will say frankly to the house that in asking what euphemistically is spoken of as a "blank cheque" we are not unmindful that we are asking very considerable from the House of Commons.
At page 4448 he said:
I am not without full realization of what is involved in the bill, but in order to meet my right hon. friend I will shorten the time to March 1 and make it clear that we have no desire to usurp powers as was suggested.
Again, at page 4449:
I need hardly say to the committee that I do this reluctantly; I do it from a sense of duty. What the right hon. gentleman said last evening as to the advisability of grants of money being limited, is so elementary I shall not do more than say that its general application in itself involves the necessity at times of exceptions.
At page 4449, again, he said:
Realizing that, understanding fully the soundness of the criticism that is urged against the principle in general and not endeavouring to minimize it, we are with great hesitancy seeking from the house these powers. ... If I were less mindful of the soundness of the criticisms that are made by the right hon. gentleman opposite as to the interference with the general principle, I would not make the observations I do.
Note the slipping of the Prime Minister. In 1931 he said that this was repugnant to him; in 1932 he is impatient with those to whom it is still repugnant. In 1931 he was apologetic; in 1932 he says that to oppose is a crime against the state. But analyze the opposition. Has any member spoken who had no right to speak? Did any member exceed forty minutes I think not. We are not asking for minority rule; all we ask for is regularity of procedure. We say to the government: Give us the details of your proposition; let us discuss them and criticize them. We may induce you to amend them and compromise somewhat, bearing in mind that last year the proposed income tax amendments were withdrawn, probablj' because of

opposition from this side of the house. The duty on magazines was reduced, probably also because of opposition from this side. We say to the government: Bring all your business before the house and let us discuss it freely, and you may depend upon it that if you defeat us on the floor of the house we shall bear the defeat with resignation: we shall be content.
I noticed with a good deal of pleasure that the Prime Minister did send over a dove, if not with an olive branch, at least with a leaf from an olive branch, when he said:
I see no harm in intimating that, instead of asking for the right to pass orders in councils with respect to peace, order and good government after the first of May, we shall specify the statute with respect to which we believe it may be essential in a time of crisis to enact reasonable regulations or orders in council.
