Mr. Speaker, in anything I shall say to-night I assure you that I am not prompted in any way by the speech made by the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Gott), who said so many uncomplimentary things about myself. I realize that the hon. gentleman has to justify an otherwise barren existence. He made one of his usual contributions to-night and talked of onions, and as he was swept along on the flood tide of his own verbosity I thought as I watched his facial contortions and violent gesticulations that he must have got some onion juice in his eye, but in fairness to the onion I would not want to put the blame for his parliamentary conduct on that lowly vegetable. After he sat down he was obviously quite exhausted. I think there was not an unuttered thought in his mind, and that being the case, he is more deserving of sympathy than of censure. As far as his prediction about my own future is concerned, he has already been proved a false prophet because he said during the last federal campaign that both the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) and myself would be defeated in our ridings, but the election results did not bear out his prognostications on that occasion. I understand fully why he did not attempt to deal with the matter under discussion, because we are discussing an important principle and I know the argument is quite beyond the capacity of the hon. member for South Essex.

The principle involved in this measure, Mr. Speaker, does not in any way relate either to farm relief or unemployment. Toryism, as in the past, is trading and trafficking on the adversity 'of those who are out of work and those who are otherwise in need of relief. If the hon. gentlemen opposite are sincere and really want to do something in a monetary way for the unemployed and the farmers in distress, all they have to do is to ask this parliament for any sum that is required, and that amount of money will be forthcoming at once with the absolute cooperation of every Liberal member on this side of the house.
But there is an ulterior motive behind this legislation, and because of that our hon. friends opposite have to muddy up the water and becloud the issue. What the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) wants, this great Moses of the Tory party, God's gift to the Canadian people, as he would have us believe, is absolute power. Under this legislation he wants to be given the power to disregard any statute of Canada and to make any new law that he likes without appealing to parliament at all. That is in contravention of every established principle of British parliamentary government. Think of it, Mr. Speaker! Over in the east block the cabinet to-morrow, if we pass this legislation, can meet and absolutely disregard any of the statutes of Canada and make any new law which the cabinet may see fit to make. What function is left to parliament if we delegate these powers to the executive? I leave that question to any fair-minded Conservative member opposite.
Apparently, after all the promises which he made in the last campaign, the Prime Minister finds himself in difficulty. He cannot in a constitutional way fulfil any part of the obligations he incurred so readily during that campaign, so now he says: What I cannot do in a conventional way I want parliament to give me authority to do in an unconstitutional way. Speaking in this house a few nights ago I suggested that if we were going to delegate any such powers it would have to be to a man of proven worth. This government has been in office now for a considerable time. This is the third session of parliament, and up to date I cannot find that one constructive suggestion has emanated from the other side of the house, not one single constructive suggestion which is fundamentally sound, and I think hon. gentlemen opposite will agree with me in that respect, particularly when we look at conditions obtaining throughout Canada to-day after this government has had every opportunity to apply thoroughly the policies which the}' advocated during the

Unemployment Continuance Act
campaign as 'being in the best interests of the people of Canada.
What, for instance, is the condition of industry to-day? We know that there are 220.000 fewer men employed. We know further that our industries are only running to forty per cent of their capacity. That situation did not obtain a few years ago under the regime of the Liberal government. What is the position of our financial institutions?
I think this is a fair test as to general conditions throughout Canada. We know that our financial institutions are in a bad way, so bad, in fact, that the Prime Minister had to invoke the powers that were vested in him under this legislation of last year in order to save our financial institutions, and by order in council he permitted the banks to file with the Department of Finance statements which were absolutely false, bolstered up, inflated statements. There must be something wrong when a condition like that obtains.
Further, by another order in council the Prime Minister allowed the insurance companies to make a retroactive valuation of the speculative stocks which they held, and not only stocks but government bonds as well. The fact that the Canadian dollar is below par and that our own government bonds are selling at a discount indicates that the policies of this government are certainly not working out in the way it was argued they would work out during the election campaign.
Take the situation as to unemployment. Hon. gentlemen opposite, those of them at all events who did not know anything about economics, probably were sincere when they told the people of this country that if elected to office they would end unemployment. They have had every opportunity to apply their policies since, and what has been the result? Instead of having 120,000 people out of work, to-day there are 550,000, and what relief is in sight? If a man loses his job to-day, picture his hopeless condition! What is he going to do about it? Is the government providing any means of employment? Has it one single constructive policy to put forward? Not one that is fundamentally sound, nothing but to give the man more of the hair of the dog that bit him.
Take the position of the farmer-and I know whereof I speak, because I have been in the rural sections in the last few days. I will tell you what is happening there. Because of the low commodity prices and the loss of markets brought about by the trade policies of this government, our farmers today are not in a position to hire help, and here is a strange anomaly as a result. These
men who cannot be employed in a gainful occupation by the farmers are crowding into the cities and towns as unemployed, where they are simply aggravating the unemployment situation, and the farmers who cannot employ these men gainfully under present conditions are going to be taxed to keep them in idleness. Some hon. gentlemen opposite will say that industry is going to bear some of this extra taxation, but I say that many of our industries that are sheltered behind tariff walls are above the civil law, and if you add to their costs of production they will simply take it out of the farmer in the prices they pay for his raw products or take it out of the consumer in the prices which he will be called upon to pay. The condition is pitiful. There is no relief in sight for the farmers. There is just a dark lane ahead of them. Picture the lot of a married man working on a farm to-day. He is not getting over $25 a month, and on that he is trying to feed and clothe his family and send his children to school, and in the country districts many little children are trudging along the sloppy roads to school without rubbers and proper footwear. Yet hon. gentlemen opposite say that they are going to help them under this farm relief legislation. Nothing of the kind. All that you are doing is to see that the big interests will have greater privileges than they ever had before. Strip this thing of all its camouflage and you find that it is nothing but an attempt to give by order in council additional privileges to the big interests.
With regard to unemployment, I do not of course blame hon. gentlemen opposite entirely for world-wide unemployment conditions. We know that the introduction of labour saving machinery, the mechanization of agriculture and industry, has contributed very largely to unemployment by the displacing of labour. But I do blame this on Toryism, that instead of the masses of the people benefiting by the cheaper methods of production by getting a corresponding increase in purchasing power through the lower prices of the products produced, Toryism allows monopolistic industries sheltered behind tariff walls to increase the prices of the products they have to sell, but the masses of the people have no corresponding increase in purchasing power.
That is what is wrong to-day in Canada, namely, lack of purchasing power; it is the root of all our trouble. The masses are being thoroughly exploited. We know this condition cannot continue to exist. The other day it was said that there were 1,125,000 automobiles in Canada, and I venture to say that because
Will the hon. member explain how it happened that he voted to abrogate the New Zealand treaty?

The abrogation of the
treaty had no direct effect upon the trading in butter between the two countries; it was the application of the eight cent tariff, that prohibitive tariff, which brought about the disaster in the Canadian industry. I know my hon. friend opposite is sincere and honest. He represents a number of dairy farmers in his constituency. May I explain the situation to him? We had for export two products: butter and cheese. Our cheese graded 96 per cent number one, and our butter 70 per cent number one. It was to act as a shock absorber, or a body behind which the government might shield itself from the ill will of an incensed electorate. My reply to the hon. member is that this government is able and willing to take the responsibility for its actions. That was the first constructive suggestion of the hon. member opposite to relieve unemployment. The second was to bring in a supply bill. Then followed ten other suggestions, some of which were constructive, but every one of which emanated from the far corner of the house. Since when has the hon. member for Vancouver Centre been authorized to speak for that independent element in the house which so frequently supports the constructive work of this government?
(Mrl Hackett.]

Hon. gentlemen opposite indulge in personalities; they ask me to speak of railways. I am willing any day to meet any of them on that topic. However until they are able to explain the inroads they made upon the finances of this country, and until they can explain their wild and extravagant administration of the railways, and the unbridled expenditure which has brought this country to the verge of bankruptejr, I feel they would be better advised to hold their peace on the railroad question.
My views may differ from those of other hon. members on this side of the house: I concede that there is a constitutional question-not a constitutional issue, but, thank God, a constitutional difference between hon. members on this side and hon. members opposite. That difference, Mr. Speaker, is the difference between the doer and the dilettante; the difference between men who are able to undertake and carry out a definite policy and men who obstruct that policy and seek by shifting methods to shield themselves from popular censure. This government made pledges that it would raise the tariff; it has carried out those pledges. It made pledges that it would relieve unemployment; it has relieved unemployment. It made pledges that it would help the farmers-and gentlemen opposite for four long weeks have stood between the farmers and that aid. This so called constitutional issue, this party cry of tiresome antiquity which has echoed through the house for the last three or four weeks is without substance and without sincerity. In the days when there was a constitutional issue in Canada there were men in the house who took the matter seriously; everyone knows to-day that it is but a subterfuge, but a futile attempt to justify in the eyes of the electorate conduct-most reprehensible conduct-of gentlemen opposite.
Order.

This constitutional cry is dead, killed by party disfavour and by popular contempt. There is something before the house, Mr. Speaker, which is of deeper and graver import than the topic which has been talked about in a most irrelevant, if not irreverent, fashion. We who have sat in the house for the last three weeks have heard dictionaries, antiquated Hansards and books of reference read to fill in the forty or twenty minutes allotted to hon. gentlemen sitting opposite. To-day we are dealing with a crisis, we have it from the mouths of hon. gentlemen opposite that there is no crisis. The fact is they have failed to realize, as demonstrated by their

Unemployment Continuance Act
conduct, that there are great issues at stake. Let hon. gentlemen opposite go into the constituencies, let them go into the cities, let them mix with the ordinary man on the street, in the store, in the market place, and they will learn that there is an issue; they will learn also that the men who are dealing with it possess public confidence. Men who are willing to dare and do, who are not bound down by any antiquated rules of procedure in their attempt to carry out the popular will, are endowed with the confidence of the public to-day.
During this debate we have had from a remote part of a remote province what I suggest to hon. gentlemen opposite is a very clear indication of popular feeling towards them and their attitude with respect to this legislation. A thoroughly agricultural community, a community which depends probably as much as any other in the whole western area upon the assistance to be received from the government in the way of seed and. feed, has said emphatically and clearly that it will not countenance the tactics of hon. gentlemen opposite. The hon. member for North Battle-ford (Mr. McIntosh) this evening told us that the gentleman who was elected for Atha-baska represented a minority of the votes. I will not attempt to contradict figures, but since he spoke I have availed myself of information at hand and I find that the hon. gentleman from North Battleford came into parliament in much the same way-and it is not to his discredit.
Not quite the same way -altogether different.

Not quite the same way? The hon. gentleman polled 7,168 votes; the candidate who came next polled 6,073 votes; and the third candidate polled 2,248 votes. My hon. friend is a minority representative by nearly two thousand votes. 1 do not hold that up to him as a reproach, but I want him to realize that under our constitution minorities do not control. That may not be a wise rule, but it is the rule under which British institutions have held sway for many a century. That rule holds just as true in parliament as it does in constituencies. In this house a substantial majority favours this legislation, that the people in Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver may have the moneys which have been promised to them; that the farmers of the west may have that seed which they hope to sow next month that they may reap a crop in the autumn, and thus recoup themselves for the misfortunes of the past three years. Do hon.
gentlemen opposite realize that we are dealing with bread and butter, with human sustenance? One hon. gentleman told us tonight of children walking along sloppy roads in footwear that was ill-suited to such conditions. Is he aware that the tactics that he and his friends have adopted stand between those children and comfort and health? Hon. gentlemen opposite have failed tc realize that this government has come into office to perform a very definite function-to alleviate suffering which is the result to a large extent of a world-wide depression. Do they realize that there is a crisis, that there is suffering, that there must be a distribution of means of support, and that this government has adopted the only means within its reach to bring assistance to these people? Do hon. gentlemen opposite understand that the whole conception and sweep of the policy of this government has been to bring help to those who are in need? Do they realize that the government dislikes this legislation just as much as they do, but that they deem it necessary, and therefore are unwilling to shirk the duty which rests upon government to minister to those who for the time being have been confided to their care?
I admit, Mr. Speaker, that there is this constitutional difference between men who fail to realize and who are unwilling to achieve, and men who do realize and who are willing to do. I do not ask hon. gentlemen opposite to cooperate; men of their point of view, who fail to realize the actualities of the day and fail to live up to the opportunity of the hour cannot be expected to cooperate with those who do realize the position and who have staked their all to relieve the trying conditions in which the Canadian people find themselves to-day. Such cooperation, Mr. Speaker, would be a defiance of the very laws of nature. I turn to hon. gentlemen on this side of the house and say: Be of high heart; your cause is good. Our right hon. leader is called a Mussolini and a czar because there is no argument to offset his policy. All that remains to hon. gentlemen opposite is the vocabulary of exaggeration and the small arms of petty politics.

To extend until the first of May, 1932, the operation of the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act. 1931, which expired on the first of March, 1932.

The resolution is not that it is expedient to introduce a bill; it is that it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the statutes of Canada, 1931. speechtext:
I have explained the
information is made up from reports furnished on printed forms supplied by the Department of Labour. Those reports are returned by the provinces. It may be there were some discrepancies. If the hon. gentleman had directed attention to it I would have seen that the matter was disposed of. I find that at page 441 of Hansard the Minister of Labour said:
The figures I have given will be subject to some flight variation when the report is tabled, which I trust will be shortly.
I think that is perhaps the explanation. I recall that the computations were hurriedly made.

The point was raised by the hon. member for Rimouski (Sir Eugene Piset)-the Prime Minister was not in at the time-with regard to what was covered by these expenditures. He pointed out that on page 5 of the report of the director of unemployment relief is contained the form of agreement between the provinces, the municipalities and the dominion. Paragraph 13 provides:
13. All public works and undertakings to which contributing may be made under the

provisions of clauses 6, 8, 9 and 10 of this agreement, are to be carried on from the date of their commencement to the date of their completion, which latter date shall not be later than the 1st day of May, 1932.
Take page 35 of the report, where a total expenditure of $20,000 is apportioned between the municipality, the province and the dominion-fifty, twenty-five and twenty-five. The dominion proportion is $5,000. Does that $20,000 represent money actually spent, or is it a commitment for the work under the agreement, the form of which I have already referred to?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think if the hon.
member will look at the top of the page he will get the information.
The columns are headed: Schedule number-description of work-total expenditure-percentage, municipal, provincial, dominion-dominion proportion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The two questions the hon. gentleman has asked are answered in this way. As to the first of May being fixed as the period of time within which the agreements were to be completed by the execution of the work, the Department of Justice ruled that with respect to matters of that kind there should be a reasonable time within which to close out the work, provided a contract, so to speak, had been let. I made personal inquiries about it when it was brought to my attention, and that was the explanation given. So far as the other point is concerned, I have not the report before me, but in some instances-and I think they are detailed in the report-expenditures actually made are distinguished from expenditures authorized. I will give the hon. gentleman an illustration. Works in the province of Quebec are being paid for by the dominion, and the province and the municipalities are each making a definite contribution. An agreement has been drawn up and executed by the province and the dominion, the only body with which the dominion has contact being the province. In the instances indicated in that report it will be found that the whole of the contemplated expenditure is expressed-that is, we will say for the sake of argument, not exceeding $20,000 by the dominion, $10,000 by the municipality and $10,000 by the province. There are other instances in that document in which the work has been actually completed and the expenditure made.
The hon. gentleman raised another question, with which I will deal, as to whether under the several agreements executed between the dominion and the provinces, obligations were created before March 1. In point of fact no fresh obligations have been created since March

Unemployment Continuance Act
1, and I should like the hon. gentleman to follow that. The department decided, as a matter of law, that a reasonable time in which to close out work that was under way, and with respect to which the contract was outstanding, was sixty days; hence the reference to May 1 with regard to which the hon. gentleman from Rimouski raised a question.
I should like to quiet my hon. friend's mind with respect to one other point. Apparently he thinks expenditures have been made without warrant and without authority, but this is the position: Some question has been raised as to whether or not, under chapter 58, there was power to pay obligations already created prior to March 1 but which came in for payment subsequent to March 1, and there was one order in council to which attention was directed by the hon. member for Quebec East, dated March 2, which authorized payment to the province of British Columbia of $500,000. That is my memory as to the amount; I speak subject to correction on that point. With respect to that, since the statute was held to be uncertain, we held up every order in council so that there would be no question, after the passing of this bill, that they could be paid. Numbers of these orders in council are now awaiting the passage of this legislation, in order that no question may be raised with respect to their payment.
Can we take it from my right hon. friend's explanation that no payments have been made or authorized since March 1, except the 8500,000 to which my right hon. friend referred?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes. I speak subject to correction, but I have looked over the matter very carefully, and I have had it looked over very carefully, and so far as I know no order has been signed constituting a charge against the consolidated revenue since March 1, except the one to which I have already referred.

Then can we take the
words "total expenditure" as they appear in the table setting out municipal works to which the dominion contributed, as meaning that this money has been actually spent?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am now advised that the cheque for $500,000, in point of fact, was held up in consequence of the question as to the certainty of that legislation.
I was referring to page 35 as a sample page, and I am asking whether the column headed "total expenditure" represents money actually spent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No. As the hon. gentleman will see by reference to the context, in
every instance starting with page 10 or page 11 these columns indicate the works that are covered in the agreements with the several provinces. That is, they were approved by the provinces and by the dominion, and if the work had been carried to completion the obligation imposed upon the province would be that mentioned in the one column, the obligation on the dominion would be that mentioned in the other column, and where there would be a municipal obligation it would be that mentioned in the first column.

This is the reason for my difficulty in understanding the report; while the column with regard to municipal and provincial works is headed "total expenditure," which in ordinary English language means that the money has been spent, the column with regard to public works-and I refer my right hon. friend to page 61-is headed "amount authorized," which I should think would be the appropriate term to use in connection with these municipal works if the expenditure was not actually made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will turn to page 35 he will see that the first item appears as number 133 in the schedule. The description of the work is "sewers and water mains in Grantham township" and the total expenditure contemplated is 820,000.
It does not say "contemplated."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is the way it was made up, and it is stated that of that expenditure the municipality is to pay 50 per cent, the province 25 per cent and the dominion 25 per cent. It is set out in this way in order that this House of Commons might have full information as to the way in which the work was to be paid for. As to page 61, that being our own transaction over which we had complete control, in that particular case the Department of Public Works was able to indicate the exact sum expended up to February 29, 1932, and that sum appears opposite the amount authorized.

What I am finding fault with is that with reference to municipal works the column is headed "total expenditure," which we are told means only the amount authorized, but when we come to page 61, which has to do with federal public works, the heading is " amount authorized," and we are told that means only the amount expended. Mr. Hereford wrote me about this and I asked the question in the house as to how much we were committed to in connection with municipal public works, because all

Unemployment Continuance Act
that appears in the report is expenditures and not commitments. Now I understand the Prime Minister to say that, keeping to page 35, the column headed "total expenditure" really means total commitment?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, it means the total
authorized expenditure under the terms of the agreement to which these several schedules were attached.
And does not really represent expenditures?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Quite so.

It represents only the
amount authorized or approved under the agreement ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: lit might well be that in some cases the sum was expended by the end of February.
But we can take it that nothing has been expended since March 1?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I said no payments had been made, but no works have been discontinued by those carrying them on under the agieements which provided for the carrying on of the works authorized.

Then I take it that in the bill which will be founded on this resolution no authorit}' will be given to contribute the full amount for which the federal government is committed in connection with municipal works which as yet have not been completed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I explained to the hon. gentleman that in my judgment that is perhaps not a correct way to state the situation. The question has been raised as to whether under chapter 58 there is ample power to complete the payments on work already started, as authorized by the agreement.
Is there really any question about that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think there might be, and those who have had to do with it in our own business think there is no doubt about it in the ordinary course. If the work is not completed within the given time there is still an obligation to pay. But in order that any difficulties might be removed and that it might not be said that there had been any effort to do this, the house is being asked for authority to make matters clear in that regard.

There is no doubt that
the Auditor General would not pass any payment made under this statute after the first of March.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think there is doubt
as to that. Provided that the work was commenced before the first of March under a contract between the province and the dominion, approved by order in council, the obligation being created and the work being completed, the obligation to pay would continue. But in order that there might be no difficulty about it the house is being asked for authority. The only order in council that was presented was one on March 2. I thought it had gone forward but I am told that as soon as the question was raised-and it was not raised by the Auditor General but by others-it was thought undesirable that the cheque should go out, and the cheque did not go out.

My right hon. friend says that I suggest there is no doubt. I feel satisfied that there would be no doubt in the mind of the Auditor General and that he would refuse to pay a cheque issued after March 1 for money authorized under the authority of the act which expired on that date.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not clear.
The Prime Minister stated that no commitments have been made since March 1. Have any payments been made since that date on old commitments?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In answer to the hon.
member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), I explained that the only order in council authorizing payment subsequently to the first _ of March was that with respect to British Columbia, on the second day of March, and which as a matter of fact was not made. And there are awaiting action of council a very large number of orders in council which represent in some instances work completed up to March 1 but which did not get here until the 10th, 12th, 13th and so on, They have not been paid.

I should like the Prime
Minister to make some explanation with regard to item No. 10 on page 12, relating to loss of stumpage due to reduction in stump-age rates. I see there is a total expenditure of $120,000 divided fifty-fifty between the dominion and the province, the dominion's share being $60,000. Can the Prime Minister inform the committee whether that is an estimate or whether that amount has been paid?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is an estimate.

In assuming responsibility
for the payment of fifty per cent of this

Unemployment Continuance Act
estimate, did the Department of Labour see to it that reasonable wages would be paid to the men in the woods in view of the reduction? I understand that wages are being paid at a very low rate. The lumbermen are getting the benefit of this reduction of $120,000 and the men are getting wages as low as S15 per month. If that is the ease, the Department of Labour ought to look into the matter before payment of this $60,000 is made. As I say, the lumbermen are getting the benefit of the reduction of $120,000 and they should certainly be in a position to pay the men more than $15 or $16 per month.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And their board.

I should like the Minister
of Labour or the Prime Minister to look into the matter, in the interest of labour, before the dominion's share is paid over.

We must be a little reasonable in regard to the rates that obtain in connection with relief. The hon. member probably forgets that there is a great difference between 'the rates of wages paid labour in connection with relief work and those that obtain in the ordinary course of business. The difference is obvious to everyone. So far as these works are concerned, where it is a matter of relief the control is very largely in the provinces, the municipalities and those concerned with caring for people in distress. With respect to federal works, in the ordinary course the rates of wages for labour are governed by the rules, practices and law that obtain in establishing, through the Department of Labour, such rates as men are entitled to.

This is not in the form of relief. It is relief in one sense, to the lumbermen, but not relief to the unemployed: If the lumbermen are going to get a bonus of this kind to encourage them to go on with operations which they otherwise would not carry on, it cannot be called relief to the unemployed. It seems to me that the Department of Labour ought to be in a position to ensure that a reasonable rate of wages will be paid before the dominion's share of $60,000 is paid. I can readily understand that in these times of distress one would not expect, in connection with relief work, that such rates of wages would be paid as were paid prior to 1930 or even 1931. But surely when the government are assisting the industry through a bonus they should see that at least reasonable wages are paid, and not starvation wages of $15 a month.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Fifteen dollars and board.
Yes, but in 1929 men were being paid $45 and $60 and board.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
in error with respect to the bonus. All that happens is that the province has abandoned the claim to stumpage, which amounts to $120,000, and the dominion government has assisted the province, as against the loss of the whole, by paying them half of it. The hon. gentleman knows how it has been carried on.

I did not mean to give
it any other interpretation. The province of New Brunswick said to the lumbermen, "We will give you a reduction in stumpage provided we can get a return from the dominion of a certain loss." That was done, and the dominion entered into this agreement with the province-I believe it is the only province in the dominion with which such an agreement was entered into. I am not criticizing the government for having entered into that agreement, and perhaps I am using the wrong term when I speak of a bonus; but I do say that where federal money is furnished in a matter of this kind we should see to it that reasonable wages are paid.

I must confess that I could not hear all that the hon. gentleman said, but the tenor of his remarks was that reasonable wages were not paid. Let me make myself abundantly clear, if I can. In all contracts that have been let in connection with this legislation, the wages were determined by the Department of Labour in the usual course. There were some works, some places of employment where people could not be established on the rate of wages that usually obtains in the Department of Public Works. With respect to that we had to do and did do the best we could in the way of trying to take care of people who were needy and in distress. Surely the hon. gentleman recognizes that. But in no case has the Department of Labour adopted an attitude that is calculated to imperil the rights of the wage earners as regards his standard of wages or standard of living. We must draw a line of demarcation between standard of wages, standard of living and relief.

In the establishment of a system of relief as contributed to by the federal government, there was made with the provinces an agreement under section 14 of which the government stipulates that the province must do so and so. It states:
A maximum work day of eight hours shall prevail on works and undertakings carried on under this agreement, unless a modification of

Unemployment Continuance Act
this requirement is previously agreed to by the Minister of Labour.
On that ipoint I am in agreement. It would be very difficult to establish an eight-hour day in a lumber camp if the work is to be properly carried on. Therefore I am not referring to that; I am reading the section merely to come , to the next point. It continues:
Fair and reasonable rates of wages shall be paid by the province and municipalities but such rates shall not be in excess of the rates required to be paid by the federal government for the character or class of work in the district.
And so forth. The reply may be made to me that this is work carried on, not by the province, but by virtue of an agreement entered into between the dominion and the provincial governments that they will become responsible for so much loss owing to the reduction in stumpage rates and therefore it can reasonably be called one of those undertakings or enterprises in. which a reasonable rate of wages shall prevail. What is the use of having an agreement such as there is under section 14 if the lumbermen are permitted to pay as low as $12 a month? A little while ago I said $15 and I can prove the statement that such low rates have been paid. On the other hand, what do we find under this very section? We find lumbermen instead of hiring, contracting with men at a very low rate of pay, a rate at which they cannot make a living in the cutting of pulpwood, and saying to these men in their agreement: In that district we have a camp opened and you shall board at it; we shall board you and charge you seventy-five cents a day for your board. The men in accepting a contract of tihat kind, have not been given the privilege of boarding themselves. Therefore, at the rate of $1.50 which they receive per cord of pulpwood, which they have to haul and pile, making their own roads, no lumberjack can handle more than two cords a day and, indeed, he is a good man who can do that. He pays 75 cents for his own board; he has to .pay the board of his horses and then at the end of the month there is nothing left for his family. It is for those reasons that I offer this, not in a critical mood;
I wish the government or the Department of Labour, if in future they are .making any such agreements as this with a province, no matter what province it may be, they will see that the labour men or lumberjacks receive a fair day's rate of wages.
I wish to direct attention to another section on page 63 of the report, where I see under the amount authorized for the county of Gloucester:
Little Shippigan-proposed wharf (estimated cost $30.000)-amount authorized, $15,000.
[Mr. Veniot.)
Perhaps the Minister of Public Works can give me the information I seek. Why has this work not been carried on? Heaven knows, unemployment in that section of the country is very acute. Among the recommendations I made in response to the request of the Department of Labour was one that this work at Little Shippigan be carried out. In 1930 I think $30,000 was estimated for that work. Tenders were called for and received, the lowest tender being $26,000. When the present government came into power in that year, they .withdrew from the expenditure of that money; they did not award a contract. I took the matter up in the bouse in 1931 and the minister promised consideration. I was pleased when in November last I saw published in the St. John Telegraph-Journal among a list of projects for the province of New Brunswick, that the Little Shippigan proposed wharf at an estimated cost of $30,000 was one of the projects agreed to or ratified by order in council. I see nothing has been done. If there is in New Brunswick a -place where unemployment is severe, it is in that section of Little Shippigan. The people there are not farmers; they farm very little; they are fishermen and last year fishing was a failure both in quantity of fish and in price obtained. There has been real hardship in that section of the county of Gloucester ever since the close of the fishing season. I should like to know why, after this work had been approved by order in council, it was not carried on. I do not think the reason was that I had recommended it; I have more faith than that in the Minister of Public Works or even in the Minister of Labour.

I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member, but surely no complaint can be made so far as this government is concerned. This work 'has been approved, and if it has not been proceeded with, why criticize this government?
Why not go on with it?

The work has been
approved. We are ready to .pay the money for it.
What is the good of the approval to the men who are out of employment unless the work is .being carried on?

When it was decided to embark upon a program of works for the relief of unemployment the engineers of the Public Works department were asked to go over the list of works which they had under consideration and make up as complete a schedule as they thought they could carry

Unemployment Continuance Act
out. My hon. friend will notice that the total expenditure for this wharf was estimated at $30,000, while the amount authorized was only $15,000. After the order in council was passed, the engineers went over the schedule of works which had been approved and were instructed to undertake only such works as, considering the season of the year and the time available, and having regard to works best suited for the relief of unemployment, they could hope to complete by the first of March. Making a study of the situation it was found that this particular work was one which could not be completed by that time, and therefore it was not undertaken. The appropriation was not sufficient in any event to complete the work, and it was thought inadvisable to undertake the work and leave it half finished.

The explanation given by the minister is not as reasonable a one as I expected from him. I have found him in my dealings with him very reasonable, but when it comes to giving an explanation for avoiding an expenditure he is not as clear as I would like him to be. If I understood him aright he said that the engineers were asked to go. over a schedule of projects and recommend only those which they felt they could complete before the fir^t of March, -and secondly that the appropriation was not sufficient to complete this work. I do not wish to introduce the element of politics, but I am afraid that I shall have to do it.
Let me say to the minister that this particular work was approved during the by-election in Gloucester county, and it was heralded all over the county. When I attempted to say that I had recommended the work to the minister and that I was glad the minister had accepted my recommendation, I was pounded by the other side as hard as a man could be pounded on the ground that I was trying to take too much credit to myself. I do not wish to imply that the approval of this work was made public for any effect it might have in that by-election, but the fact is that the knowledge that it had been approved came out just at that time. Let me go further and say to the minister that other projects were approved and contracts let without the full amount of the cost of the work having been voted. That has been the practice all through, and it is a proper one. Sufficient money is voted to permit of the minister entering into a contract, and then, when the tenders are in, the amount is known and the minister can provide the further amount required in a supplementary estimate. All that he would have to do would be to get another order in council
passed. A contract could have been let for this work in the month of November last, and the work could have been gone on with and relief given to these people. The work of providing the lumber and gathering the stone for the ballast for the wharf could have been gone on with during November, December, January and February. The work of construction in that secluded and protected area within Miscou harbour could have been gone on with in the winter time and could have been constructed, as has often been done in the shallow waters, on the ice, sinking their cages with ballast. In that way the work could have continued right along.
By day labour?

No, by contract. The
government is carrying on a lot of public works to-day under contract for the relief of unemployment. I would not suggest that a work of this amount, $30,000, be carried on by day labour. The government is perfectly justified in calling for tenders, providing the wage-earner is protected under the contract, which matter is looked after by the Department of Labour. If that work had been carried on the municipality of Gloucester to-day would have been relieved of the demand which is being made for direct aid in that district. The county of Gloucester has sent in an estimate for direct aid amounting to $110,000. That will give hon. gentlemen some idea of the distress in that county. A great many of the people in Gloucester county are fishermen; in fact, I think I am safe in saying that one-half of the population depends upon the fishing industry. All along that coast where this wharf was to be built, there is no farming. There is a shifting, sandy soil, and the people do very little farming, but they fish. As I said before, the fishing season was a failure both as to quantity and price, and I now appeal to the government to take the necessary steps to proceed with this work as soon as it is possible to do so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We cannot until the
statute passes.

Oh, yes. The hon. gentleman could have done it by awarding the contract at the time that approval was given to the project, and if the contract had been let the work could have been carried on beyond the first of March because under the agreement the time can be extended by order in council to the first of May. Even Bill No. 58 is being extended by order in council. It may be quite true that the work is held up now, but between now and the time when the bill passes

The resolution now before us is rather scarred. In its original form the resolution read as follows:
Resolved that it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the statutes of Canada, 1931, striking out the word "March" in section 8, and substituting the word "May" therefor, and on the proposed motion of Mr. Weir (Melfort): "That this question be now put."
That was the resolution as it stood yesterday afternoon. The amendment by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) is to extend until May 1, 1932, the operation of the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act of 1931 which expired on March 1, 1932. Now, Mr. Chairman, I ask this question: By what process of law can this extension be made? Notwithstanding the wonderful legal attainments -and they are well known-of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice how, may I ask, can we extend until May 1, 1932, the operation of the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act of 1931, which expired on March 1, 1932? It is not a question of asking leave to introduce a new statute or to revive an old one, but to extend the operation of a statute which, on the admission of the government itself, is dead and has expired. I challenge the Minister of Justice, who at one stage of this debate said he would be heard, but who has kept a most religious silence, to pledge his standing as an eminent jurist at the bar, and say that there is some process of law whereby the operation of an expired statute can be extended.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes; this parliament can
extend a statute any time it wishes. In that

Unemployment Continuance Act
respect parliament is clothed with every power.
That may be so, if we desire so to stultify ourselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is the only question.

I do not wish to be a
party to that stultification.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Very well, that is your
answer.

This government is
omnipotent; the Prime Minister has stated that he has a comfortable working majority and that he cares not-n-o-t or n-o-u-g-h-t, whichever word you choose to use-for the rights of minorities. Therefore, with an accommodating majority at his back willing to pass the proposed legislation, of course it will be passed. However, they will have to take that step on their own responsibility.
We will.

The responsibility will
be on their own shoulders, if they wish to place themselves in that awkward position. In their eyes might is right. If they wish to extend the operation of the statute, they are welcome to do so, but it is their responsibility.
Why worry about it?
I wish the hon. member would tell us what is worrying him.
Nothing.

Well then, why does he not keep quiet? What has surprised me throughout this debate is that hon. gentlemen sitting on the other side have kept wonderfully and religiously silent; from the one hundred and twenty of them we have heard nothing; but the moment we put a finger on a sore spot they jump up like so many marionettes, as was said this afternoon. But up to the present not one of them has dared to say where he stands on this question.

V ou got it on the
vote, didn't you?
If they have so much to say, why in mercy don't they stand up and make a speech?
You make one.

If the hon. gentleman
who is so prone to make these interruptions would speak for twenty minutes only once during the session I would listen to him and say he might interrupt as often as he liked for the remainder of the session. But he is
satisfied merely to grunt, to make these disturbing noises now and then. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) says we may extend the operation of a dead statute, but I do not want to be associated with this strange fashion of legislating. I do not know if any of his colleagues, if for instance my hon. friend the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ryckman) who is also a member of some standing at the bar, is prepared to subscribe to the idea that we may legally extend the operation of a dead statute. On the opposite side there are many men of eminent legal attainments, and I am quite sure that one of the reasons why they have not endorsed the view of the Minister of Justice is that they have some respect for their standing a-t the bar. When the Prime Minister introduced this motion he said he wished to extend the operation of the act. Quite properly he stated even last year that he had some hesitation as to the constitutionality of this procedure. I quote from page 4279 of Hansard of last session:
I will say frankly to the house that in asking what euphemistically is spoken of as a "blank cheque" we are not unmindful that we are asking very considerable from this House of Commons.
I pay the right hon. gentleman this tribute to his legal acumen, that he knew he was skating on thin ice, but was willing to take a chance. This session I find that at page 335 of Hansard he said:
I would not ask this power from any parliament except very reluctantly.
Again I pay him the tribute that he had some hesitation because of his legal attainments and felt that he was on very thin ice. The Prime Minister smiles. I do not wonder at his smiling when he realizes the position he has placed himself and those who follow him. If it were not for the fact that he has such a very accommodating majority behind him he would not dare take such a position. I am confident that before the Privy Council he would never venture to propound such an unsound theory. The Prime Minister brought this motion down for the purpose of amending the statute, but as we hammered away at it he finally found himself on the road to Damascus-and the light started to shine. In the course of the last few days he said-I am quoting from page 1407 of Hansard:
The government is determined it would renew the statute.
The Prime Minister did not say the government were going to amend the statute, but that they were going to renew it. No

Unemployment Continuance Act
one in this house knows better than the right hon. gentleman that there is an absolute difference between renewing and amending a statute. At page 1409 he again used the word "renew." He also said:
I desire that this statute be revived.
Not that its operation be extended, but that it be revived. He knows there is an absolute difference between reviving and amending a statute. At page 1410 he said:
Shall the Canadian parliament through a government supported by a majority in this house-
And a very accommodating majority.
-be permitted to reenact by proper words the legislation of last session?
Not to amend, not to extend the operation,
but to reenact, to do something absolutely new7, to start de novo. Now watch how the Prime Minister is coming down very reluctantly, but he is finally driven to this point. At page 1418 he said:
The use of the appropriate words to enable the principle of the legislation to be made effective.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the right hon. gentleman, even with all his legal attainments, took some time to find out that his magic was dead, that there was no process under British law whereby a dead statute could be amended, but instead of coming out frankly he has hedged all along. Now he asks that the operation of this expired statute be extended until the first of May, 1932.
There are many other reasons why I would have opposed the passing of this motion, but I think that one of the soundest reasons is to take the stand that you cannot extend by any recognized legal means-although you may do it by a majority of this kind-the operation of a dead statute.

As we know,
under this bill power will be given to the governor in council to pass orders in council up to the first of May. May I ask: will any such orders in council have any effect after the first of May, or will their operation cease entirely on that day?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Except for the purpose of enabling payment of balances unpaid on contracts not completed; they would cease to be valid on the first of May.

The Prime Minister refers to orders in council that may relate to money payments. There may be orders in council relating to other matters. I assume such orders in council will have no force and effect after the first of May?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman is quite correct. It is proposed in the bill that orders in council shall forthwith be laid on the table of the house.

I understand
that. With regard to payments between now and the first of May is it the intention of the government to initiate new contracts or to make fresh commitments which will run beyond the first of May, or will everything be confined to the first of May?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is a question, Mr. Speaker, which at the moment I cannot answer. For instance, a few days ago a delegation from the city of Quebec waited upon the government, and my right hon. friend's colleagues 'who were present suggested that there should be an extension of time in connection with work which was to be done in that city, which climatic conditions had made it impossible to complete during the winter. The hon. member for Gloucester urged that since spring was coming on, and unemployment was so serious, the matter should be so dealt with. I could not say definitely that pressure of conditions such as those existing in Quebec, for instance, might not have some effect. I was quite convinced, I may say frankly, by the statement of the mayor of Quebec city that they were unable to complete that work, and might not be able to complete it by May 1. They asked for an extension of time, the matter being already reduced to a contract for which authorization was given in the report tabled in this house. I cannot answer that question beyond saying that the necessities of the particular case would have to govern.

My right hon. friend refers to a contract, the terms and extent of which are already known. My question refers to something which at the moment is not known. Between now and May 1 will the administration make any new contracts which will run beyond May 1?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question which has already been asked once or twice on the orders of the day. Does the relief commission at Regina take seed grain liens on all crops resultant from seed grain advances, and if so when are they payable?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The question of the character of the security taken by the commission is something between the commission and the provincial authorities, and the dominion has nothing whatever to do with it beyond the fact that we are given to understand, and do understand in advancing the money, that the commission is adequately protecting itself with respect to the crops. I cannot say whether a lien is taken on one or two crops, but my understanding is that the lien has to do with the first year's crop, and in some instances with the second year's crop, but the money is loaned to the province of Saskatchewan, which province is responsible for the arrangements made between the relief commission and the farmers with respect to the collection of the sums so advanced.

My understanding
is that this government has already agreed to the use of the relief commission as a collection agency for this government. If there is an understanding of that nature I think the government should be aware of what kind of security is being taken from the farmers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The relief commission is
a provincial body set up by the provincial government, and as such it is subject to provincial control. They made the arrangement with themselves. All we did was to supervise, so far as we could, the proper expenditure of the money in the manner indicated in this house. The form of security they may take, in order that they may be able to repay to the dominion the moneys advanced, is not our business.

I do not see why
we cannot get this information now; we have asked for it several times.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I shall be glad to give
the hon. gentleman any information I have.

In the application
for relief made by a farmer in Saskatchewan, the farmer faithfully promises to pay to the Saskatchewan Relief Commission, on behalf of His Majesty the King in the right of the Dominion government, on or before such and such a date, all advances made to him by way of relief or seed grain, at the value and prices stated by the commission. I take it that the
obligation is assumed by the commission to collect for the seed grain as well as for the relief on behalf of the government of Canada, and with all due respect to my right hon. friend I do feel that someone in the government should be able to give this information.
I think the Minister of Agriculture was asked the question, but he was not in a position to answer it very definitely. Before going further I think we should have this question answered I have before me a bill which recently passed the Saskatchewan legislature incorporating the Saskatchewan Relief Commission, and the way in which our farmers are being hog-tied in connection with these seed grain and feed advances is simply terrible. I do not think we should go further without complete information in this regard.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will answer the hon.
gentleman, and I hope he hears me. First, the province of Saskatchewan is making the arrangements, through its relief commission, with the individual farmers with respect to seed grain; second, the seed grain is being provided by the Dominion government; third, the province is undertaking to repay to the Dominion government the money expended in the purchase of seed grain; fourth, my understanding-and I am not advised fully-is that the legislature of Saskatchewan is taking such steps as are regarded as essential for the purpose of enabling it to secure repayment of the advances so made.

Then are we to
understand that this government accepts no responsibility at all for the terms imposed upon the farmers by the Saskatchewan government or the relief commission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.
I suppose in Regina they will say the same thing, that they have no responsibility either.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.
I submit that there is an individual as well as a joint responsibility resting on both governments in regard to the terms upon which these farmers get this seed grain.

There are a
number of questions we should like to ask in connection with this resolution, but I understand that when the bill is in committee ample opportunity will be given for discussion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Quite so, and I think it will expedite matters when the committee has the bill before it. The only reason I have
Questions

remained until this hour is because some safeguards have been suggested to me, but I believe it will be much clearer when the house is in committee. Then we will be able to answer any questions that may be brought forward.
Resolution as amended reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Bennett thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 24, respecting unemployment and farm relief.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
Mr. Bennett moved the adjournment of the house.
What will be the business this afternoon?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We will continue with
this bill. If we finish it we will take the motion with regard to supply which is now pending.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 4.20 a.m. (Wednesday).
Wednesday, March 30, 1932
